title: AC Temperature Saving Calculator (26° vs 18°) | Wattlyst
meta: See how much you can save each month by raising your AC temperature, as a percent and in units, for your old and new set points and monthly AC units.
author: ali-ahmad

sections.h2: AC temperature saving calculator: what the number means
p: The result is an estimate from a rule of thumb: each degree you raise the set point cuts the AC's units by roughly 6%. The rule exists because the compressor works against the gap between outdoor and indoor temperature; a smaller gap means less heat to pump out of the room. It is not a measured value for your AC, your room or your city, so the per-degree figure is an input you can change.
Use the result to compare settings and decide, not as a promise of a bill. The only exact saving is a measured one: note the meter reading over a few similar days at each setting.

sections.h2: AC at 26 degrees: how much does it save?
p: Moving from 22 °C to 26 °C saves about 24% of the AC's units by the rule of thumb, 58 units a month for an AC that uses 240. From 18 °C the rule gives 48%, but treat that as an upper figure: at very low settings many ACs already run flat out and never reach the set point, so the real gap between the two settings is smaller than the numbers on the remote.
A ceiling fan running with the AC makes a warmer setting feel cooler, because moving air helps sweat evaporate. That is why the higher setting is usually comfortable with the fan on.

sections.h2: Best AC temperature to save electricity
p: The warmest setting that keeps you comfortable is the cheapest. For most people with a fan running that is the 26 °C used as the default here, which is also the common energy-saving advice. Every degree lower costs roughly another 6% of the AC's units.

A low setting does not cool the room faster: the AC cools at the same rate until it reaches the setting, it just keeps going longer. Setting 18 °C instead of 24 °C to cool down quickly only adds about 36% more units by the same rule.

sections.h2: Does the rule work for inverter and non-inverter ACs?
p: The rule of thumb is used for both. An inverter AC slows its compressor as the room nears the setting, so a warmer setting lets it run slower for longer; a non-inverter AC switches its compressor off more often. In both cases the units fall as the set point rises. The size of the effect varies with the model, the insulation and the outdoor heat, which is why the per-degree figure is editable.

faq.q: How much electricity does raising the AC temperature save?
faq.a: Roughly 6% of the AC's units for each degree raised, by a common rule of thumb. From 22 °C to 26 °C that is about 24%, 58 units a month for an AC using 240.

faq.q: Is 26 degrees the best AC temperature to save electricity?
faq.a: It is the usual energy-saving advice and comfortable for most people with a ceiling fan on. Any warmer setting you are comfortable with saves more; each degree lower costs roughly another 6% of the AC's units.

faq.q: How much do I save running the AC at 26 instead of 18?
faq.a: The rule of thumb gives 48% of the AC's units, 115 units a month for an AC using 240. Treat it as an upper estimate: at very low settings many ACs run flat out without reaching the set point.

faq.q: Does a low setting cool the room faster?
faq.a: No. The AC removes heat at the same rate whatever the setting; a lower setting only makes it run longer and use more units.

faq.q: How do I find how many units my AC uses a month?
faq.a: Use the AC units calculator: average kW × hours a day × days. A plug-in energy meter or the daily reading on a smart meter over a few days gives a measured figure.

faq.q: How much money will I save?
faq.a: Units saved × your slab rate. Because Pakistani bills are billed in slabs, a saving that keeps you below a slab limit can save more than the units alone suggest; check the full bill with the electricity bill calculator.

key_facts: Each degree Celsius you raise an AC's set point saves roughly 6% of the AC's units; this is a planning rule of thumb, and the real saving depends on the room, the outdoor heat and the AC.
Moving a 1.5 ton inverter AC that uses 240 units a month from 22 °C to 26 °C saves about 58 units a month by the rule of thumb.

Going from 18 °C to 26 °C saves about 48% of the AC's units by the same rule; over such a large gap the figure is the least certain, because at very low settings many ACs run flat out without ever reaching the set point, so the real difference between the two settings is smaller.
The saving applies to the AC's units only, not to the whole bill; fans, the fridge and lights use the same units at any AC setting.
mistakes: Applying the saving to the whole bill. It applies to the AC's own units; the fridge, fans and lights do not change.
Treating the rule of thumb as exact. The 6% per degree is an approximation; your AC, room and weather decide the real figure.
Setting the AC very low to cool the room faster. It cools at the same speed and simply runs longer; by the same rule the drop from 24 °C to 18 °C costs about 36% more units.
Raising the setting but closing the fan. Without moving air the warmer setting feels less comfortable, and people turn it back down.

examples.title: 1.5 ton inverter AC from 22 °C to 26 °C
examples.text: 6% per degree for the degrees raised = 24%; 240 units a month × 24% = about 58 units saved a month.

examples.title: From 18 °C to 26 °C
examples.text: The rule gives 48% of the AC's units, 115 units a month. Over this large a gap, treat it as an upper estimate: at very low settings many ACs never reach the set point.

examples.title: A cautious estimate at 3% per degree
examples.text: With half the default rule, the same move from 22 °C to 26 °C saves 12%, about 29 units a month. Use this when your room is well shaded and the AC rarely runs at full power.

examples.title: Turning the AC down from 24 °C to 18 °C
examples.text: Lowering the set point costs units instead of saving them: about 36% more, roughly 86 extra units a month for an AC that used 240.

content.answer: Raising the AC from 22 °C to 26 °C saves roughly 24% of the AC's units, about 58 of 240 units a month. The rule of thumb is saving = about 6% per degree raised × degrees raised × the AC's monthly units. It is an approximation, not a measurement of your AC.

formula.text: Units saved = monthly AC units × min(1, per-degree saving × (T_new − T_old))
lines: T_old, T_new = set temperature now and the new one, in °C
per-degree saving = approximate share of AC units saved per degree raised (editable rule of thumb)
monthly AC units = the AC's own units a month, from the AC units calculator or a plug-in meter
If T_new is lower than T_old, the same rule gives the extra units instead of a saving

content.safety: Changing the set point is safe. If the AC trips its breaker, smells of burning or the outdoor unit makes grinding noises, switch it off and call a qualified AC technician or a licensed electrician.
